levels.description: First steps in Mandarin: greetings, numbers, basic verbs and questions.

topics.title: Pinyin Tones
topics.description: Train your ear for the four tones — the foundation of Mandarin

guide.intro: Mandarin uses pitch to tell words apart. The same syllable in a different tone is a different word — get tones in your ear before you build sentences.

sections.text: Why tones matter
English uses pitch for emotion ("REAL-ly?" vs "really."). Mandarin uses pitch for meaning. "mā" (mom) and "mà" (scold) are not the same word — they're as different as "cat" and "dog".
The four tones + neutral
When you practice, exaggerate. Tones feel embarrassing at first — that's how you know you're doing them right.
Sandhi: tones that shift
Two real-world tweaks: (1) when two 3rd tones meet, the first becomes 2nd: nǐ + hǎo → ní hǎo. (2) 不 (bù) becomes bú before a 4th tone (bú shì). (3) 一 (yī) becomes yí before 4th, yì otherwise.

lessons.title: Meet the four tones
lessons.description: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th + neutral

exercises.prompt: How many tones does Mandarin have (not counting neutral)?
exercises.explanation: Four tones — 1st (flat), 2nd (rising), 3rd (dip), 4th (falling). Plus an unstressed neutral tone.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 1st tone (high and flat)?
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) over the vowel signals 1st tone — held high and steady.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 2nd tone (rising)?
exercises.explanation: The acute accent (´) signals 2nd tone — pitch rises like "huh?"

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 3rd tone (dip down then up)?
exercises.explanation: The háček (ˇ) signals 3rd tone — pitch dips then comes back up.

exercises.prompt: Which mark shows the 4th tone (sharp falling)?
exercises.explanation: The grave accent (`) signals 4th tone — short, falling, often emphatic.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 妈 is high and flat — the 1st tone. It means "mother."

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 马 (horse) dips down then back up — the 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 骂 (scold) falls sharply from high to low — the 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: tone to its meaning
Type the pinyin for "horse" (3rd tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 马 = mǎ. Use the ˇ mark for 3rd tone (or write "ma3" in numeric pinyin).

exercises.prompt: Mandarin's neutral tone is best described as ___
options: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
A 5th tone with its own contour
exercises.answer: Unstressed and light, often on the second syllable
exercises.explanation: Neutral tone has no mark — said quickly, lightly. Common in particles (吗, 呢) and repeated syllables (妈妈).

exercises.prompt: Which syllable is most likely neutral tone?
exercises.explanation: In doubled family terms like 妈妈, 爸爸, 哥哥 — the second syllable is neutral.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "mother" (1st tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 妈 = mā. First tone, held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which character matches the 2nd tone (rising) ma-syllable?
exercises.explanation: 麻 (má) is 2nd tone — rising. Means "hemp" or "numb".

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for "to scold" (4th tone, ma-syllable):
exercises.explanation: 骂 = mà. Fourth tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: Tap the syllable you hear
exercises.explanation: 麻 (má) — 2nd tone, rising. Means hemp.

exercises.prompt: Two syllables can have the same letters and the same initial — only the ___ makes them different words.
exercises.explanation: Tones are phonemic in Mandarin — they distinguish meaning.
妈 (mā) — flat high tone, means "mother."

exercises.prompt: The mark ¯ over a vowel signals tone number ___
exercises.explanation: The macron (¯) is the 1st tone mark — held high and flat.

exercises.prompt: Which tone has the háček (ˇ) mark?
exercises.explanation: The háček ˇ marks 3rd tone — pitch dips then rises.

lessons.description: Flat-high vs rising

exercises.prompt: 1st tone is held high and flat. 2nd tone does what?
exercises.explanation: 2nd tone rises from mid to high — same melody as English "huh?"

exercises.prompt: bā vs bá — which one is the 2nd tone?
exercises.explanation: bā 八 (eight) is 1st tone, flat. bá 拔 (to pull) is 2nd tone, rising.

exercises.prompt: fā vs fá — which means "to send / hair" (1st tone)?

lessons.title: 3rd vs 4th tone
lessons.description: Dipping vs falling

exercises.prompt: How does the 3rd tone move?
options: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.answer: Dips down then comes back up
exercises.explanation: Mid → low → mid. In careful speech the dip is dramatic; in quick speech it's often a low "half-3rd".

exercises.prompt: mǎi vs mài — which means "to buy"?
exercises.explanation: 买 mǎi = buy (dipping). 卖 mài = sell (falling). Remember: 卖 has the extra 十 on top — "goods piled up to sell."

exercises.prompt: kàn means "to look/watch." What tone is it?
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — sharp falling. (kǎn 砍 "to chop" with 3rd tone is a different word.)

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 买 dips and rises — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 卖 falls sharply — 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — sharp, falling 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 那 nà = that — 4th tone. Compare 哪 nǎ = which — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: 3rd vs 4th — pair to meaning
Type the pinyin for "to look/watch":
exercises.explanation: 看 kàn — 4th tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: You hear a single short, falling syllable. What tone is it most likely?
exercises.explanation: Short + falling = 4th. Native speakers often shorten 4th tone in casual speech.

exercises.prompt: 4th tone moves ___
options: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.answer: Sharp falling from high to low
exercises.explanation: 4th tone is the dramatic crash — high to low, abrupt.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 卖 ("to sell"):
exercises.explanation: 卖 mài — 4th tone, sharp falling.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 那 ("that"):

买 mǎi — 3rd tone, dipping.

exercises.explanation: 哪 nǎ — 3rd tone, dipping.

exercises.explanation: Same initial m + ai. Tones change meaning entirely.

exercises.prompt: Which tone is often shortened in fast speech?

exercises.answer: 妈 麻 马 骂
exercises.explanation: 妈 (1st) → 麻 (2nd) → 马 (3rd) → 骂 (4th). The classic teaching set.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 看 ("look/watch"):

lessons.title: 3rd-tone sandhi
lessons.description: How 你好 actually sounds

exercises.prompt: What happens when two 3rd tones meet (3rd-tone sandhi)?
exercises.explanation: 3 + 3 → 2 + 3. So nǐ + hǎo is written nǐ hǎo but said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: 你好 is written nǐ hǎo. What does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: First 3rd tone shifts to 2nd. Pinyin keeps the original marks; your mouth does the shift.

exercises.prompt: 很好 (hěn hǎo, "very good") — what does it sound like?
exercises.explanation: Two 3rd tones in a row → first becomes 2nd. Said hén hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 你好 — the most common hello. Note the sandhi: written nǐ hǎo, said ní hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 很好 — said hén hǎo because of 3rd-tone sandhi.

exercises.prompt: How is sandhi written in pinyin?
exercises.explanation: Standard convention: write nǐ hǎo, say ní hǎo. The shift is in your mouth, not on the page.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones in 我也好 (wǒ yě hǎo, "I'm also good"). The first two shift. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Chains of 3rd tones: most become 2nd, only the last stays 3rd. wǒ yě hǎo → wó yé hǎo.

exercises.prompt: written vs spoken
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 可以 ("can / may") — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across pauses/sentence breaks?
options: Always, every time two 3rd tones touch
Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.answer: Only within a single word or tight phrase
exercises.explanation: Sandhi follows the rhythm of the phrase. If you'd naturally pause between the syllables, no shift.

exercises.prompt: 3-3 sandhi means ___ becomes ___
exercises.explanation: 3+3 → 2+3. Written marks stay; the change is spoken.

exercises.prompt: How is 很好 actually pronounced?
exercises.explanation: 3+3 → 2+3. Written hěn hǎo, spoken hén hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase undergoes 3-3 sandhi?
exercises.explanation: Only when two 3rd tones touch within a phrase.

exercises.prompt: Write "you good" using two characters
Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 可以 — written kě yǐ, said ké yǐ (sandhi).

exercises.prompt: Sandhi marks are ___
options: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.answer: Mental — not shown on the page
exercises.explanation: Standard convention keeps the original 3rd-tone marks. The shift lives in the mouth.

exercises.prompt: Three 3rd tones — only the LAST stays 3rd. Type the spoken version of 我也好:
exercises.explanation: Chains shift: most syllables become 2nd, only the last keeps 3rd.

exercises.prompt: Does sandhi apply across a pause/comma?
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 我很好 with 3-3 sandhi: wó hěn hǎo.

exercises.prompt: Which is NOT affected by 3-3 sandhi?
exercises.explanation: 明天 mingtiān — 2nd + 1st. No two 3rd tones to clash.

lessons.title: 不 and 一 sandhi
lessons.description: When bù becomes bú and yī becomes yí/yì

exercises.prompt: 不 (bù) means "not." What's its default tone?
exercises.explanation: 不 is normally 4th tone — bù. It only shifts before another 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: 不 + 是 (shì, "is") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú shì "is not."

exercises.prompt: 不 + 来 (lái, 2nd tone, "come") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays 4th: bù lái "not come."

exercises.prompt: 一 (yī) means "one." Before a 4th tone like 个 (gè), it becomes...
exercises.explanation: 一 + 4th → yí. So 一个 is yí ge in speech.

exercises.prompt: 一 + 起 (qǐ, 3rd tone, "rise") — what do you say?
exercises.explanation: Before non-4th tones (1st, 2nd, 3rd), 一 becomes 4th: yì qǐ "together."

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 不是 — 不 shifts to 2nd tone before 是 (4th).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 一个 = yí ge — one (thing). 个 is neutral in speech but counts as 4th for sandhi.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 一起 = yì qǐ — together. 一 became 4th before 3rd-tone 起.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 要 (yào, 4th, "want") in speech?
exercises.explanation: Before a 4th tone, 不 becomes 2nd: bú yào "don't want / don't."

exercises.prompt: When does 一 NOT shift tone?
options: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.answer: When standing alone or saying numbers in sequence
exercises.explanation: Counting (yī, èr, sān...) or year numbers (一九九九) keeps 一 as 1st tone. Sandhi only kicks in when 一 leads into another syllable as part of a meaning unit.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 不 + 对 (duì, 4th, "correct")?
exercises.explanation: Before 4th tone, 不 shifts to 2nd: bú duì.

exercises.prompt: Before any non-4th tone, 不 stays ___
exercises.explanation: 不 + 1st/2nd/3rd → bù (4th, unchanged). Only 不 + 4th → bú.

exercises.prompt: 一 + 天 (tiān, 1st, "day") becomes ___
exercises.explanation: Before non-4th tones, 一 shifts to 4th: yì tiān.

exercises.prompt: How is 一年 (one year) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 2nd (年 nián) → 一 becomes 4th: yì nián.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 不 + 2nd-tone 来 → unchanged: bù lái.

exercises.prompt: 不 changes tone only when followed by ___
exercises.explanation: Sandhi rule for 不: only before 4th tones does it shift to 2nd.

exercises.prompt: How is 一千 (one thousand) spoken?
exercises.explanation: 一 + 1st (千 qiān) → 一 becomes 4th.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: Before 4th tone 要, 不 → bú.

exercises.prompt: In counting (yī, èr, sān…) what tone does 一 keep?
exercises.explanation: Sandhi doesn't apply when 一 is standing alone or counting.

exercises.prompt: Order: bú shì → before this 4th-tone character, 不 shifts to 2nd

topics.title: Pinyin Sounds
topics.description: The tricky consonants and vowels of pinyin — the ones English doesn't have

guide.intro: Pinyin is the romanization that lets you type, look up, and pronounce Mandarin. Most letters do what you'd expect — but a handful are traps for English speakers.

sections.text: Initials: where sound starts
Mandarin has three pairs that English speakers mix up: zh/ch/sh (retroflex — curl your tongue back) vs z/c/s (sibilant — tongue flat). Plus j/q/x — like Italian's c/g — always followed by i or ü.

rows: j in 'jar' with tongue curled back

sections.text: j / q / x — the i/ü trio
j, q, x are softer than zh, ch, sh — tongue stays forward. They only ever appear before i or ü. After j/q/x, ü is written as plain u (so 居 is jū, but the vowel is really ü).
qù sounds like "chü" — NOT "q-you" or "tsoo." The q is a soft "ch" and ù is a rounded "ee" with pursed lips.
Finals: the trap vowels
Some finals don't match their spelling. -ian sounds like "yen," not "yan." -uan after j/q/x/y is really -üan (so 元 yuán = "yu-en"). -eng has a back "ung" feel vs -en which is light and forward.

lessons.title: Initials: zh/ch/sh vs z/c/s
lessons.description: Retroflex (tongue curled) vs flat sibilants

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between zh and z?
options: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
z is retroflex; zh is flat
exercises.answer: zh is retroflex (tongue curls back); z is flat
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh = tongue curled back (retroflex). z/c/s = tongue flat. Easy to mix up; speakers in southern China often merge them.

exercises.prompt: 知 ("to know") is zhī. How is 资 ("resource") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī uses the retroflex zh; 资 zī uses flat z. Same vowel, different tongue position.

exercises.prompt: Which English sound is closest to Mandarin c (as in 词 cí)?
exercises.explanation: c is the "ts" cluster — no h, no curl. Don't read it as English "c."

exercises.prompt: 吃 ("to eat") is chī. How is 词 ("word") spelled?
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī uses retroflex ch; 词 cí uses flat c. Common minimal pair.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: Retroflex zh — tongue curled back.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 四 sì — flat s, no tongue curl, 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 是 shì — retroflex sh, tongue curls back.

exercises.prompt: retroflex vs flat partners
Type the pinyin for 是 ("is"):
exercises.explanation: 是 shì — retroflex sh, 4th tone. The most common verb "to be."

exercises.prompt: Which is a fact about southern-China accents?
options: They distinguish zh/z more carefully than the north
They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.answer: They often merge zh/z, ch/c, sh/s
exercises.explanation: Many southern speakers (Shanghai, Taiwan, etc.) don't distinguish retroflex from flat — they pronounce 是 closer to sì. Standard Mandarin (北京话) keeps them apart.

exercises.prompt: Which sound requires tongue curled back?
exercises.explanation: zh/ch/sh are retroflex — tongue tip curls back.

exercises.prompt: Which is the flat sibilant partner of sh?
exercises.explanation: s is the flat partner; sh is retroflex.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 吃 ("to eat"):
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī — retroflex ch, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 词 ("word"):
exercises.explanation: 词 cí — flat c, 2nd tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 私 sī — flat s, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Native speakers from which region most consistently distinguish zh/z?
exercises.explanation: Northern Mandarin (Beijing) keeps retroflex distinct from flat.
吃 chī — retroflex ch.

exercises.prompt: c in Mandarin pinyin sounds like ___
exercises.explanation: c = ts, never English c. No aspiration mistake.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 资 zī — flat z, 1st tone.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 知 ("to know"):
exercises.explanation: 知 zhī — retroflex zh, 1st tone.

lessons.title: Tricky j/q/x + i/ü
lessons.description: When 'u' is really 'ü' and q isn't English q

exercises.prompt: j, q, x can ONLY be followed by which vowels?
exercises.explanation: Hard rule: j/q/x never appear before a, o, u, e by themselves. They only pair with i (as in ji, qi, xi) or ü (written u, as in ju, qu, xu).

exercises.prompt: 居 is spelled "jū." What's the actual vowel sound?
options: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.answer: ü (rounded ee — say ee with pursed lips)
exercises.explanation: After j/q/x/y, ü drops its dots: jū looks like "ju" but is really jü. Make ee with rounded lips.

exercises.prompt: 去 ("to go") is qù. How would you describe the sound?
exercises.explanation: q is a soft, forward "ch" — not the English q. ù is the rounded-ee. So qù is more like "chü" than anything in English.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is actually pronounced with ü?
exercises.explanation: ju, qu, xu, yu are all really jü, qü, xü, yü. zhu, chu, shu, zu, cu, su use real u.

exercises.prompt: What does the x in Mandarin sound like?
options: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.answer: soft sh — tongue forward, like a German "ich" softened
exercises.explanation: x = a forward, light "sh." Tongue near the roof of the mouth, no curling. 谢 xiè ("thanks") and 学 xué are common.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: qù — soft ch + ü, 4th tone.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: xué — soft x + ü-e diphthong, 2nd tone (rising). "To study/learn."

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: jī — soft j (like "jee"), 1st tone. Don't confuse with retroflex zhī.

exercises.prompt: Type the pinyin for 学 ("study/learn"):
exercises.explanation: xué — that x is the soft, forward "sh," and ue is really üe.

exercises.prompt: Why is the ü written as plain u after j, q, x, y?

topics.title: How Characters Work
topics.description: Chinese characters are made of reusable pieces — learn to spot them

guide.intro: Chinese characters look intimidating but they're built from a small set of reusable pieces. Once you see the pattern, learning new characters speeds up.

sections.text: Characters are made of pieces

Almost every Chinese character is a combination of smaller components. Some components are simple characters in their own right; others (radicals) only appear as parts of larger characters. Recognizing the pieces makes the whole easier.

rows.translation: good
bright
forest
rest (a person leaning on a tree)

sections.text: Radicals as meaning clues

About 200 "radicals" group characters by meaning. If a character contains 氵 (water), it likely relates to water (rivers, drinking, thirst). 心 (heart) → emotions. 口 (mouth) → speech and eating. The radical doesn't tell you the whole meaning, but it points you in the right neighborhood.

rows: 河 river, 海 sea, 江 river, 渴 thirsty
林 forest, 树 tree, 桥 bridge
想 think, 爱 love, 急 urgent
吃 eat, 喝 drink, 叫 shout/call
你 you, 他 he, 们 plural-marker
她 she, 好 good, 妈 mom

sections.text: When you see a new character, guess at the radical first. If it has 氵 you'll be roughly right calling it water-related — that's enough to remember it.

lessons.title: Characters are made of pieces
lessons.description: Components and meaning-compounds

exercises.prompt: 好 ("good") is made of which two components?
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo = 女 + 子 — woman with child. A traditional mnemonic for "good."

exercises.prompt: 明 ("bright") is made of which two components?
exercises.explanation: 明 míng = sun + moon = bright. One of the most famous "meaning-compound" characters.

exercises.prompt: 林 ("forest") is made of what?
exercises.explanation: Two 木 (tree) = 林 lín (forest/grove). Three trees = 森 sēn (dense forest). Repeat for emphasis.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to rest" (a person leaning on a tree)?
exercises.explanation: 休 xiū = 亻 (person) + 木 (tree). Pictorial: a person resting against a tree.

exercises.prompt: character to its components
你 ("you") contains which component on the left?
exercises.explanation: 亻 is the "person" radical (a flattened form of 人). It shows up in many person-related characters: 你, 他, 们, 休, 体.

exercises.prompt: Why do components matter for learning?
options: They don't — just memorize each character whole
They group characters by meaning and pronunciation, making recall faster
They only matter for traditional characters
exercises.answer: They group characters by meaning and pronunciation, making recall faster
exercises.explanation: Most characters fall into a pattern: one piece hints at meaning (radical), one hints at sound. Knowing this turns rote memorization into educated guessing.

exercises.prompt: 她 ("she") differs from 他 ("he") only by replacing which component?
exercises.explanation: 他 tā = person + 也 (the default "he"). 她 tā = woman + 也 (the gendered "she"). Same sound, different left piece.

exercises.prompt: 好 = 女 + ___ . Type the second component:
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo = 女 (woman) + 子 (child). The traditional reading: a woman with her child = "good."

exercises.prompt: 森 ("dense forest") is made of how many 木?
exercises.explanation: 森 sēn = three 木. One tree = 木. Two = 林 (forest). Three = 森 (dense forest). Chinese character design at its most direct.

exercises.prompt: The character 男 ("man/male") combines ___
exercises.explanation: 男 = field + strength. Traditional: "the one who works the field with strength."

exercises.prompt: 好 = 女 + 子. 女 means ___
exercises.explanation: 女 = woman/female. Look for 女 on the left of many female-related characters.

exercises.prompt: Three trees stacked together (森) means ___
exercises.explanation: 一木 (tree) → 二木 (林, grove) → 三木 (森, dense forest).
林 lín — two 木. Forest/grove.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to rest"?
exercises.explanation: 休 xiū — person leaning on a tree (亻 + 木) = rest.
明 míng = 日 (sun) + 月 (moon) = bright.

exercises.prompt: Which radical is on the LEFT of 你?
exercises.explanation: 亻 is the side form of 人 (person) — appears in many pronouns/people characters.

exercises.prompt: Order the pieces of the character 好
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 好 hǎo — 3rd tone, dipping. Combination character: woman + child.

exercises.prompt: Why do components matter?
options: They hint at meaning AND sometimes sound — making memorization easier
exercises.answer: They hint at meaning AND sometimes sound — making memorization easier

lessons.title: Common radicals
lessons.description: 氵 water, 木 wood, 心 heart, 口 mouth

exercises.prompt: 氵 is the radical for what?
exercises.explanation: 氵 is the "three-drops" form of 水 shuǐ (water). Appears on the left of water-related characters: 河 (river), 海 (sea), 渴 (thirsty).

exercises.prompt: Which character does NOT contain the water radical 氵?
exercises.explanation: 山 shān is its own pictograph (three peaks) — no 氵. 河, 海, 江 all use 氵 because they involve water.

exercises.prompt: 木 is the radical for what?
exercises.explanation: 木 mù = tree. As a radical, it marks things made of wood or related to trees: 桥 bridge, 树 tree, 林 forest.

exercises.prompt: What does 心 mean (as a radical)?
exercises.explanation: 心 xīn = heart. Appears in characters for emotions and thinking: 想 think, 爱 love, 急 urgent, 怕 afraid.

exercises.prompt: 口 means "mouth." Which character uses it?
exercises.explanation: 吃 chī (eat) has 口 on the left — eating uses the mouth. Also 喝 (drink), 叫 (shout/call), 唱 (sing).

exercises.prompt: radical to its meaning
character to its radical
Which radical would you expect to find in a character meaning "to sing"?
exercises.explanation: 唱 chàng (to sing) has 口 — singing uses the mouth. Pattern repeats: 叫 (shout), 喊 (yell), 喝 (drink), 吃 (eat).

exercises.prompt: Which radical would you expect in 爱 ("love")?
exercises.explanation: 爱 ài contains 心 in the middle (slightly hidden in modern simplified form, very clear in traditional 愛). Love = a heart matter.

exercises.prompt: Why are radicals useful for looking up characters?
options: They're alphabetized by radical in dictionaries
Older paper dictionaries indexed all characters by their radical and stroke count
Both of the above are true
exercises.answer: Both of the above are true
exercises.explanation: Before digital tools, you found a character by identifying its radical, then counting remaining strokes. Knowing radicals = knowing how to navigate the language.

exercises.prompt: Where does the 氵 radical usually sit?
exercises.explanation: Most radicals appear on the left or top.

exercises.prompt: The radical for "mouth" is ___
exercises.explanation: 口 (kǒu) = mouth. Found in eat, drink, shout, sing.

exercises.prompt: Which character likely has the 木 radical?
exercises.explanation: 桥 has 木 — bridges were made of wood.

exercises.prompt: Which character means "to drink"?
exercises.explanation: 喝 hē — has 口 (mouth) because drinking uses the mouth.

exercises.context: The full form — 氵 is the side-form radical
exercises.explanation: 水 shuǐ — water. As a radical, becomes 氵.

exercises.prompt: The radical 心 means ___
exercises.explanation: 心 (xīn) = heart. Found in characters about emotion: 想, 爱, 怕.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 水 shuǐ — 3rd tone.

exercises.prompt: Why does 唱 (sing) have 口?
exercises.explanation: Pattern: anything you do with the mouth tends to have 口.

exercises.prompt: Which character is built from THREE trees?
exercises.explanation: 森 = three 木 = dense forest.

exercises.prompt: Order the radicals: water, wood, heart, mouth
exercises.answer: 氵 木 心 口

lessons.title: Reading by radical clue
lessons.description: Guess unfamiliar characters from their radical

exercises.prompt: 渴 (kě) contains 氵 (water). What's the likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 渴 kě = thirsty. The 氵 radical hints at water; the rest gives the sound (曷 hé/gě). Confidence trick: see 氵 → bet on water.

exercises.prompt: 想 (xiǎng) has 心 (heart) on the bottom. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 想 xiǎng = to think, to want, to miss. The heart radical signals "mental/emotional" — exactly right.

exercises.prompt: 桥 (qiáo) has 木 (wood) on the left. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 桥 qiáo = bridge. Old bridges were wood — hence the radical. Pattern: 木 = something built from / made of wood.

exercises.prompt: 唱 (chàng) has 口 (mouth) on the left. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 唱 chàng = to sing. Anything you do with your mouth — speak, eat, shout, sing — tends to have 口.

exercises.prompt: 湖 (hú) has 氵 . What is it?
exercises.explanation: 湖 hú = lake. Big body of water → 氵 radical is the giveaway.

exercises.prompt: 忙 (máng) has 忄 (the side form of 心). Likely meaning category?
exercises.explanation: 忙 máng = busy (mentally occupied). 忄 is the side-form of 心 — same heart radical, different shape. Shows up in 快 (happy/fast), 怕 (afraid), 怒 (angry).

exercises.prompt: 喝 (hē) has 口. Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 喝 hē = to drink. Mouth radical 口 + sound clue from 曷. Compare with 渴 kě (thirsty, water radical).

exercises.prompt: unfamiliar character → likely meaning category
You see 树 — a character with 木 on the left. The character means ___
exercises.explanation: 树 shù = tree. The 木 radical is the giveaway. Use this trick on every new character: find the radical, narrow the meaning.

exercises.prompt: Final tip: when you meet a new character, what should you do first?
options: Memorize the whole thing as one shape
Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.answer: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.explanation: Radical → category → narrow guess from context. Far more efficient than rote memorization. The other components often hint at sound.

exercises.prompt: You see 河 — it has 氵. The likely meaning is ___
exercises.explanation: 河 hé = river. The 氵 radical screams "water-related."

exercises.prompt: 怕 (pà) has 忄 (heart). Likely meaning?
exercises.explanation: 怕 pà = afraid. Emotion → heart radical.

exercises.prompt: A character with 木 on the left is most likely related to ___
exercises.explanation: 木 radical = wood/tree-related: 树, 林, 桥, 板.
湖 hú = lake. Water radical gives it away.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 想 xiǎng — to think. Heart radical at bottom.

exercises.prompt: If you see 忄 on the left of a character, you should guess ___
exercises.explanation: 忄 is the side form of 心 — used in many emotion words.

exercises.prompt: 树 contains 木. The most likely meaning is ___
exercises.explanation: 树 shù = tree. The 木 radical is the giveaway.

exercises.prompt: 吃 has 口 because eating uses the ___
exercises.explanation: 口 radical points to mouth-related actions: eat, drink, shout.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 桥 qiáo — bridge. Has 木 radical.

exercises.prompt: First step when meeting a new character?
options: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category
exercises.answer: Identify the radical to guess the meaning category

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.

sections.text: How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 吗 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 吗 = 你好吗? ("are you good?").

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一万 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 万 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 两
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 两 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.

sections.text: Asking how many
几 (jǐ) asks "how many?" for small expected counts (under ~10). 多少 (duō shǎo) asks "how much/many?" for any quantity, including money and big numbers.

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.

rows.translation: I drink tea.
He eats rice.
I love you.

sections.text: Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.

rows.translation: I am a student.
I am good. (no 是!)

sections.text: Negation: 不 vs 没
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 没 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

rows.source: 我 不 喝 茶。
rows.translation: I don't drink tea.

rows.source: 我 没 有 钱。
rows.translation: I don't have money.

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

rows.source: 昨天 我 吃 米饭。
rows.translation: Yesterday I ate rice.

rows.source: 明天 我 吃 米饭。
rows.translation: Tomorrow I will eat rice.

exercises.prompt: the right negation: ___ 喝 茶。(I don't drink tea.)

exercises.prompt: the right negation: 我 ___ 有 钱。(I don't have money.)

Why does Mandarin distinguish 哥哥 vs 弟弟 instead of using one word for "brother"?

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.

rows.translation: I go / I am going.
He goes.
We go.
I went yesterday.

sections.text: Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜欢
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.translation: I want coffee. (I'll have)

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.
I like coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。
rows.translation: I ate. / I have eaten.

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Days, hours, and when things happen

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 点 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.

rows.translation: 3 o'clock

sections.text: Time-words come first
In Mandarin, time goes before the verb. Compare:

rows.source: 我 明天 去 学校。
rows.translation: I am going to school tomorrow.

rows.source: 他 今天 不 来。
rows.translation: He is not coming today.

sections.text: A handy memory trick: Chinese says time in big-to-small order — year, month, day, hour, minute. The opposite of how dates are spoken in English.

topics.title: Questions
topics.description: Who, what, when, why, how

guide.intro: Mandarin questions are unusually friendly to learners — there's no auxiliary "do/does", no inversion. The word order stays the same as a statement.

sections.text: The 吗 particle
For yes/no questions, take a statement and add 吗 (ma) at the end. That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

rows.translation: You drink tea.

rows.source: 你 喝 茶 吗？
rows.translation: Do you drink tea?

sections.text: Question words stay put
For information questions (who, what, where), put the question word exactly where the answer would go. No fronting like English.

rows.translation: Who are you? (You are who?)
What are you drinking?
Where are you?
Why is he coming?

sections.text: Common question words
A-not-A questions
A second way to ask yes/no questions: repeat the verb with 不 between. It's a touch more direct than 吗.

rows.source: 你 是不是 学生？
rows.translation: Are you a student or not?
Do you drink tea or not?

sections.text: Don't mix patterns: 你是不是学生吗？ is wrong. Pick one of the two question forms.

exercises.prompt: Build: "Who is he?"

What does "为什么" literally translate to?
exercises.explanation: 为 = for/because, 什么 = what. "For what reason" = why.

exercises.prompt: "什么意思" (shén me yì si) means ___
exercises.explanation: 意思 = meaning. The handy phrase to ask the meaning of a word: ___ 什么意思?

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Type the character meaning "who":
exercises.explanation: 谁 shéi — who.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
In Mandarin, question words go ___
exercises.explanation: 你是谁? Literally "you are who?"

exercises.prompt: Build "What are you reading?"
To ask the meaning of a word, use "___ 什么意思?"

exercises.prompt: "哪国人" means ___

exercises.prompt: What does "多少钱" mean?
What does "几个" (jǐ ge) mean?
"怎么样" (zěn me yàng) means ___
the question word
When asking the price of something, you would use ___
exercises.explanation: 钱 (qián) = money. 多少 fits any quantity — perfect for prices, which can be small or large.

exercises.prompt: Build: "How many people are in your family?"
exercises.answer: 你 家 有 几 个 人

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
"几岁" (jǐ suì) is for asking ___'s age
exercises.explanation: 几岁 expects a small number — only fits children. For adults, use 多大 (how big) — "how old."

exercises.prompt: What does "怎么样" do in conversation?
options: Asks "how about it?" or "what do you think?"
exercises.answer: Asks "how about it?" or "what do you think?"
exercises.explanation: Versatile phrase — used to ask opinion, suggest plans, or check up on someone. "今天怎么样?" = "How was today?"

exercises.prompt: Build: "How much is this?"

exercises.prompt: What word turns a statement into a yes/no question?

exercises.prompt: How do you ask "Are you good?"
Build "Do you want tea?"

exercises.explanation: 你喝茶 → 你喝茶吗? That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

exercises.prompt: the question particle
Statement: 你是中国人. Add ___ to make it a yes/no question.
exercises.explanation: Sentence-final 吗 turns any statement into a yes/no question.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
What's the "A-not-A" form of "do you drink tea?"

exercises.prompt: Why is 你是不是学生吗? wrong?
options: You can't combine A-not-A with 吗 — pick one
是不是 should be 不是不
exercises.answer: You can't combine A-not-A with 吗 — pick one
exercises.explanation: A-not-A and 吗 are two ways to form yes/no questions. Don't mix them.

exercises.prompt: Build A-not-A: "Are you a student?"
exercises.answer: 你 是 不 是 学生

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Statement: 他是学生. The yes/no question (with 吗) is: 他是学生 ___
exercises.explanation: Add 吗 at the end. Yes/no questions don't change word order.

exercises.prompt: "What is this?" — which is right?
exercises.explanation: Standard Mandarin word order: subject + verb + question word: 这 + 是 + 什么. Putting 什么 first is a Chenglish slip from English "What is..."

exercises.prompt: "Do you have time?" — correct version?
exercises.explanation: Yes/no questions add 吗 to the END of a statement: 你有时间吗？ The full sentence stays in normal order; only 吗 is added.

exercises.prompt: Type the particle that turns a statement into a yes/no question:
exercises.explanation: 吗 ma — yes/no question particle, sentence-final.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear

exercises.explanation: Repeat verb with 不 between: 要不要.

exercises.prompt: Build the A-not-A question "do you go?"
exercises.answer: 你 去 不 去

exercises.prompt: Can you combine A-not-A with 吗?
exercises.explanation: Use one or the other — never both.

exercises.prompt: "出租车" (chū zū chē) means ___

exercises.prompt: the routine phrase

topics.title: Completed actions
topics.description: 了 for what just happened, 过 for what you've ever done

guide.intro: A1 introduced 了 briefly. A2 is where it really earns its keep. There are also two siblings to learn — 过 (experience) and 还没 (not yet) — that round out talking about the past.

sections.text: 了 — completed action
Tack 了 onto a verb to mark that the action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to a past tense, but technically it's an aspect marker — the action is complete, not necessarily long ago.

rows.translation: I am eating.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。
rows.translation: I ate / I have eaten.
He came / he's here.

sections.text: Negation: 还没 (not yet)
Don't pair 了 with 不/没. To say "haven't done it", drop 了 and use 还没 (hái méi):

rows.translation: I haven't eaten yet.
He hasn't come yet.

sections.text: 过 — experience marker
过 (guò) tags a verb as "have you ever done this in your life?" — it's about experience, not completion. Compare:

rows.source: 我 吃 过 北京 烤鸭。
rows.translation: I have eaten Peking duck (sometime).

rows.source: 我 吃 了 北京 烤鸭。
rows.translation: I ate Peking duck (just now).

sections.text: Rule of thumb: 了 = the action is wrapped up. 过 = at some point in your life this happened. They occasionally co-occur but you'll mostly pick one.

topics.title: Aspect markers: 了 / 过 / 着
topics.description: Three little particles, three big meanings — sort them out.

lessons.title: 了 — completed action
lessons.description: 了 marks a completed action, not English past tense.

exercises.prompt: What does the 了 in "我 吃 了" signal?
exercises.explanation: 了 (le) marks completion — the eating happened and is done. It is NOT a tense marker.

exercises.prompt: Best English for "我 已经 吃 了"?
options: I already ate / I have already eaten
exercises.answer: I already ate / I have already eaten
exercises.explanation: 已经 (yǐ jīng) = already; pairs naturally with completion 了.

exercises.prompt: Build "I ate dinner"
exercises.answer: 我 吃 了 晚饭

exercises.prompt: Fill the particle: "她 买 ___ 一 本 书" (She bought a book)
exercises.explanation: Action completed → 了 right after the verb.

exercises.prompt: Which is correctly using 了 for a completed action?
options: 我 去 了 学校
我 了 去 学校
了 我 去 学校
我 去 学校 吗 了
exercises.answer: 我 去 了 学校
exercises.explanation: Verbal 了 sits right after the verb: 去 了.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 喝 了 = drank (completed).

exercises.prompt: True or false: 了 in "我 吃 了" is the same thing as English "-ed"
exercises.explanation: 了 marks completion, not past time. "明天 我 吃 了 饭 就 去" (tomorrow, after I've eaten, I'll go) uses 了 in a future context.

exercises.prompt: "我 看 完 了 电影" means ___
acceptableAnswers: I have finished watching the movie
exercises.explanation: 看 完 = finish watching; 了 reinforces completion.

exercises.prompt: Build "He drank the water"
exercises.answer: 他 喝 了 水

exercises.explanation: 写 了 = wrote (completion); 三 封 信 = three letters.

exercises.source: 我 已经 吃 了

lessons.title: 过 — experiential
lessons.description: 过 means "have done it (at some point)" — an experience, not a single event.

exercises.answer: I've been to Beijing (at some point)
exercises.explanation: 过 (guo) marks experience — at least once, ever.

exercises.prompt: How does "我 去 了 北京" differ from "我 去 过 北京"?
options: 了 = a specific completed trip; 过 = have-been-there experience
exercises.answer: 了 = a specific completed trip; 过 = have-been-there experience
exercises.explanation: 我 去 了 = I went (one specific time). 我 去 过 = I've been (at some point).

exercises.prompt: Fill the particle: "你 吃 ___ 北京 烤鸭 吗?" (Have you ever eaten Peking duck?)

exercises.explanation: "…before / at some point" = experiential 过.

lessons.title: 着 — ongoing state
lessons.description: 着 marks a persisting state, not a progressive action.

exercises.prompt: Best English for "门 开 着"?
options: The door is open (and stays open)
exercises.answer: The door is open (and stays open)
exercises.explanation: 着 (zhe) = the resulting state persists. Compare to 门 开 了 = the door opened.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence describes a held / ongoing state?
options: 他 拿 着 一 本 书
他 拿 了 一 本 书
他 拿 过 一 本 书
他 要 拿 一 本 书
exercises.answer: 他 拿 着 一 本 书
exercises.explanation: 拿 着 = is holding (state). 拿 了 = picked up / took (event).

exercises.prompt: Fill the particle: "她 穿 ___ 一 件 红 衣服" (She's wearing a red shirt)
exercises.explanation: Wearing = ongoing state → 着.

exercises.prompt: Build "The window is open" (state)
Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 拿 着 = holding.

exercises.prompt: "墙 上 挂 着 一 张 照片" — what does this describe?
options: Someone is hanging a photo right now
A photo hangs / is hanging on the wall
A photo fell off the wall
exercises.answer: A photo hangs / is hanging on the wall
exercises.explanation: 挂 着 + locative = stative description of how something is.

exercises.prompt: Which is the WRONG way to say "I'm reading a book right now"?
options: 我 在 看 书
我 正在 看 书
我 看 着 书
我 在 读 书
exercises.answer: 我 看 着 书
exercises.explanation: For action in progress use 在/正在. 着 is for stative descriptions.

guide.intro: Real Chinese shopping is fast and friendly. Three phrases get you 80% of the way there: 多少钱 (how much), 太贵了 (too expensive), and 给我 (give me).

sections.text: Money words
Spoken Chinese uses 块 (kuài) for the main currency unit; written and formal Chinese uses 元 (yuán). They're the same value — like "buck" vs "dollar". 毛 (máo) and 分 (fēn) are tenths and hundredths.

topics.title: Comparisons
topics.description: A is bigger than B — the 比 pattern

guide.intro: English uses "-er" or "more" for comparisons. Mandarin uses 比 (bǐ) — a single particle that does the same job, with a fixed word order: A 比 B + adjective.

sections.text: Basic pattern: A 比 B + adjective

rows.source: 我 比 他 高。
rows.translation: I am taller than him.

rows.source: 苹果 比 香蕉 便宜。
rows.translation: Apples are cheaper than bananas.

rows.source: 今天 比 昨天 热。
rows.translation: Today is hotter than yesterday.

sections.text: Don't add 很 / 不 / 是 to a 比 sentence. "我 比 他 很 高" is wrong — drop 很. The comparison itself does the work.
Even more: 更
Add 更 (gèng, "even more") before the adjective when comparing to an already-strong baseline:

rows.source: 他 比 我 更 高。
rows.translation: He is even taller than me.

sections.text: The most: 最
最 (zuì) before an adjective means "the most". No 比 needed — it's a superlative.

rows.translation: He is the tallest.

rows.source: 我 最 喜欢 茶。
rows.translation: I like tea the most.

sections.text: Negative: A 没有 B + adjective
To say "A is NOT as ___ as B", flip to 没有 (méi yǒu, "doesn't have"):

rows.source: 我 没有 他 高。
rows.translation: I am not as tall as him.

topics.title: Connecting ideas
topics.description: And, but, because, so — stitch sentences together

guide.intro: Up to now most sentences have been one thought. A2 is where you start chaining: "I went and then I ate", "It rained but I went", "I'm tired because I worked". Mandarin makes this easy — a small set of connectors does most of the heavy lifting.

sections.text: 然后 — and then
然后 (rán hòu) chains two events in time. Use it to narrate sequences.

rows.source: 我 起床，然后 吃 早饭。
rows.translation: I get up, and then I eat breakfast.

sections.text: 但是 / 可是 — but
Both mean "but" with no real difference; 可是 is a touch more conversational.

rows.source: 我 想 去，但是 我 没 时间。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng qù, dànshì wǒ méi shíjiān.
rows.translation: I want to go, but I don't have time.

sections.text: 因为...所以 — because...so
Mandarin often uses both halves where English uses just one ("I'm tired BECAUSE I worked" → 因为 我 工作 了，所以 我 很 累).

rows.source: 因为 下雨，所以 我 没 去。
rows.pinyin: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù.
rows.translation: Because it was raining, (so) I didn't go.

sections.text: You can drop one half if context is clear: "因为 下雨，我 没 去" works too. The full pair just sounds slightly more emphatic.
或者 vs 还是 — both mean "or"
Easy mix-up. 或者 (huò zhě) goes in statements ("I want tea or coffee"). 还是 (hái shi) goes in questions ("Do you want tea or coffee?").

rows.source: 我 想 喝 茶 或者 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng hē chá huòzhě kāfēi.
rows.translation: I want to drink tea or coffee. (statement)

rows.source: 你 想 喝 茶 还是 咖啡？
rows.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng hē chá háishi kāfēi?
rows.translation: Do you want tea or coffee? (choice question)

lessons.title: At the airport

exercises.prompt: the airport word
What does "护照" (hù zhào) mean?
Which means "to board (a plane)"?
the airport area
What does "起飞" (qǐ fēi) mean?
Build "My flight is delayed by two hours"
exercises.answer: 我 的 航班 晚点 了 两 个 小时
exercises.explanation: 晚点 (wǎn diǎn) — "behind schedule, delayed". The duration follows the verb.

exercises.prompt: "行李 超重 了" means "The luggage is ___"
At the gate the announcement says "请 乘客 登机". What should you do?
exercises.explanation: 乘客 = passenger; 请 ... 登机 = please board. This is the boarding call.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.spokenText: 请出示您的护照和登机牌
options: 请出示您的护照和登机牌
请出示您的护照和身份证
exercises.answer: 请出示您的护照和登机牌
exercises.explanation: 出示 (chū shì) — "to show / present". Standard phrase at security and gate.

exercises.prompt: Build "Please put your luggage on the conveyor belt" with 把
exercises.answer: 请 把 行李 放 在 传送带 上
exercises.explanation: Classic 把 + location pattern at security: take the luggage AND put it on the belt.

exercises.prompt: "转机" (zhuǎn jī) means a ___ flight
Your friend says 我 的 航班 取消 了. Which English sounds natural?
exercises.explanation: English-L1 trap: forgetting the -ed past participle. 取消 + 了 → "is cancelled" (state) or "was cancelled" / "got cancelled" (event).

exercises.prompt: Which one means "flight number"?
Build "Please show me your boarding pass"
exercises.answer: 请 给 我 看 一下 你 的 登机牌

exercises.prompt: "行李 ___ 重 了" — fill the missing word for "too"
What's the natural reply to "您 的 行李 有 几 件？"
options: 我 有 两 件
我 是 两 件
exercises.answer: 我 有 两 件

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Build "Where is the boarding gate?"
exercises.answer: 登机 口 在 哪里

lessons.title: Booking & buying tickets
lessons.description: Reservations and one-way vs round-trip

exercises.prompt: What does "订机票" (dìng jī piào) mean?
the ticket term
Build "I want to book a one-way ticket"
exercises.answer: 我 想 订 一 张 单程 票
exercises.explanation: 张 (zhāng) is the measure word for tickets and flat objects.

exercises.prompt: Which means "to change a ticket"?
exercises.explanation: 改签 (gǎi qiān) — change the date/time of a ticket. 退票 = refund, 出票 = issue ticket.

exercises.prompt: the booking word
Build "I want to book a round-trip ticket to Shanghai"
exercises.answer: 我 想 订 一 张 去 上海 的 往返 票
exercises.explanation: "To Shanghai" becomes a 去 上海 的 modifier sitting before 往返 票.

exercises.prompt: What's the difference between "网上订" and "窗口订"?
options: 网上订 = book online; 窗口订 = book at the counter
exercises.answer: 网上订 = book online; 窗口订 = book at the counter

exercises.prompt: "靠 窗 的 座位" means "___ seat"
Build "Please give me an aisle seat" with 给
exercises.answer: 请 给 我 一 个 靠 走道 的 座位
exercises.explanation: 靠 走道 的 = aisle (literally "the side-of-the-aisle one"). 给 marks the recipient (you).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.spokenText: 我想订一张明天去北京的机票
options: 我想订一张明天去北京的机票
我想订一张今天去上海的机票
我想退一张明天去北京的机票
我想买一张明天去北京的火车票
exercises.answer: 我想订一张明天去北京的机票

exercises.prompt: How would you politely ask the price?
exercises.explanation: 请问 + ... + 一 张 — fully polite: "May I ask, how much for one ticket?"

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.spokenText: 我 知道 这 个 航班
options: 我 知道 这 个 航班
我 字典 这 个 航班
我 之 道 这 个 航班
我 自 道 这 个 航班
exercises.answer: 我 知道 这 个 航班
exercises.explanation: Minimal pair: 知道 (zhī dào, retroflex zh-) vs 字典 (zì diǎn, dental z-). Listen for the tongue-curl on zh.

exercises.prompt: What does "单程 票" (dān chéng piào) mean?
Build "I want to change my ticket to tomorrow"
exercises.answer: 我 想 把 票 改 到 明天

exercises.prompt: "经济 ___ " (jīng jì ___) — fill in for "economy class"

Tap what you hear
Build "Can I get a refund on this ticket?"
exercises.answer: 这 张 票 可以 退 吗

exercises.prompt: How would you ask the price of a round-trip ticket?
options: 往返 票 多少 钱
退 票 多少 钱
exercises.answer: 往返 票 多少 钱

exercises.prompt: Build "I'd like a non-smoking double room"

exercises.explanation: 间 (jiān) is the measure word for rooms. 无 烟 = smoke-free.

The hotel asks "您 预订 了 吗？" — what are they asking?
Build "The Wi-Fi in my room doesn't work"
exercises.answer: 我 房间 的 Wi-Fi 用 不 了
exercises.explanation: V 不 了 — "can't be used / can't V (due to a problem)". A common spoken complaint pattern.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
exercises.explanation: 多 住 一 晚 — "stay one more night". 多 + verb + amount = a useful pattern at hotels.

exercises.prompt: Which means "single room"?

exercises.prompt: Build "There's no hot water in my room"
exercises.answer: 我 房间 没有 热水

晚 退 房 可以

lessons.title: Lost & asking for help
lessons.description: When things go wrong on the road

exercises.prompt: What does "我 迷路 了" (wǒ mí lù le) mean?
Build "My luggage is gone"
exercises.answer: 我 的 行李 不见 了
exercises.explanation: 不见了 — "is gone / missing" — a very common pattern.

exercises.prompt: "请 帮 我" (qǐng bāng wǒ) means "Please ___ me"
Tap the phrase you hear
exercises.explanation: 丢 (diū) — to lose. "My passport is lost."

exercises.prompt: the help phrase
Pick the passive form: "My wallet got stolen"
options: 我 的 钱包 被 偷 了
我 把 钱包 偷 了
我 的 钱包 偷 了 我
我 偷 钱包 了
exercises.answer: 我 的 钱包 被 偷 了
exercises.explanation: Theft is the textbook 被 sentence — bad thing happening TO the patient.

exercises.prompt: Build "Could you please call the embassy for me?" with 给
exercises.answer: 你 能 给 我 打 电话 给 大使馆 吗
exercises.explanation: Two 给 in a row — first marks beneficiary (me), second marks recipient of the call (embassy).

exercises.prompt: You missed your flight. Which is right?
options: 我 错过 了 飞机
我 没 上 飞机
我 不 去 飞机
我 把 飞机 错过
exercises.answer: 我 错过 了 飞机
exercises.explanation: 错过 (cuò guò) — "miss" (a chance, a flight, a person). The 了 marks completion.

exercises.prompt: Build "I lost my passport, can you help me?"
exercises.answer: 我 把 护照 丢 了 你 能 帮 我 吗
exercises.explanation: 把 + 丢 + 了 — natural 把 sentence because 丢 changes the object (you no longer have it).

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Which sounds most natural for "I'm lost, can you tell me where the subway is?"
options: 我 迷路 了，请 问 地铁 在 哪里？
我 迷路 了，地铁 哪里？
我 不 知道 路，地铁？
地铁 在 哪？我 是 迷路。
exercises.answer: 我 迷路 了，请 问 地铁 在 哪里？

exercises.prompt: Which means "embassy"?
Build "Please call the police for me"
exercises.answer: 请 帮 我 报 警

exercises.prompt: "小心" (xiǎo xīn) means "be ___"

lessons.title: Train station vs airport
lessons.description: Different vocab for different platforms

exercises.prompt: the train word
What does "候车室" (hòu chē shì) mean?
Which word is for trains, NOT planes?
exercises.explanation: 动车 (dòng chē) — bullet train (D-train). 登机牌 = boarding pass; 航班 = flight; 起飞 = take off.

exercises.prompt: Build "My high-speed train leaves at 3 pm"
exercises.answer: 我 的 高铁 下午 三 点 出发

exercises.prompt: "硬卧" (yìng wò) is a kind of ___ on a Chinese train
airport word with the train equivalent
Build "Which platform does this train leave from?"
exercises.answer: 这 趟 车 在 几 号 站台 出发
exercises.explanation: 趟 (tàng) is the measure word for a trip / a run of a train. 几 号 = which number.

exercises.prompt: At a Chinese train station, what does "安检" mean?
exercises.explanation: Chinese train stations have full bag scanners — 安检 is the same word as at airports.

exercises.prompt: Tap what you hear
Which is faster?
exercises.explanation: 高铁 — high-speed rail, typically 300+ km/h. 普通 列车 is the regular slow train.

exercises.prompt: Build "I prefer the train over the plane"
exercises.answer: 比 起 飞机 我 更 喜欢 火车
exercises.explanation: 比 起 X ("compared to X") + 我 更 ... — a B1 comparative pattern.

exercises.prompt: Which means "train station"?
Build "I'd like to buy a high-speed train ticket"
exercises.answer: 我 想 买 一 张 高铁 票

exercises.prompt: "硬 座" (yìng zuò) is a kind of ___ on a Chinese train
What does "卧铺" (wò pù) mean?

exercises.prompt: Pick the right reply: "几号 站台?"

exercises.prompt: the currency

exercises.prompt: Which means "today's exchange rate"?
Build "How much is one US dollar in RMB?"
exercises.answer: 一 美元 等于 多少 人民币
exercises.explanation: 等于 (děng yú) — "equals". The most natural way to ask exchange ratios.

Build "Can I pay with WeChat?"
exercises.answer: 可以 用 微信 付款 吗

exercises.prompt: The clerk says "请 在 这 里 签 名". What do they want?
exercises.explanation: 签 名 (qiān míng) — sign your name.

exercises.prompt: Which means "to withdraw money"?

topics.title: The 把 construction
topics.description: Putting the object first to talk about what you do TO it

guide.intro: 把 (bǎ) is one of the most distinctive features of Mandarin grammar. It moves the object before the verb to say "take X and do something to it". You'll hear it constantly — and English doesn't have a clean equivalent.

sections.text: The basic shape

Normal Chinese order is Subject–Verb–Object. With 把, you reorder to Subject–把–Object–Verb–(extra). The "extra" part is crucial — 把 sentences almost never end on a bare verb. There has to be a result, location, or change attached.

rows: 我 把 门 关 上
他 把 苹果 吃 了
请 放 书 在 桌子 上
请 把 书 放 在 桌子 上

sections.text: When to use 把
Use 把 when you want to emphasize what HAPPENS TO a specific, known object — moving it, finishing it, changing it, putting it somewhere. Both speaker and listener know which object you mean.

rows.source: 我 把 作业 做 完 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ bǎ zuòyè zuò wán le.
rows.translation: I finished the homework.

rows.source: 请 把 窗户 打 开。
rows.translation: Please open the window.

rows.source: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Tā bǎ bēizi dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: He broke the cup.

sections.text: If you can't say what HAPPENS TO the object, don't use 把. "我 把 苹果 喜欢" is wrong — 喜欢 (like) doesn't change the apple.
What can't follow 把
把 needs a verb that physically affects the object. Verbs that don't qualify: feeling/perception verbs (爱, 喜欢, 觉得, 知道), existence verbs (有, 是), and most stative or motion-only verbs (来, 去, 走).

rows.source: 我 喜欢 这 本 书。
rows.translation: I like this book. (NOT 我 把 这 本 书 喜欢)
He knows the answer. (NOT 他 把 答案 知道)

sections.text: Negation: 没 / 不 goes BEFORE 把

rows.pinyin: Wǒ méi bǎ zuòyè zuò wán.
rows.translation: I didn't finish the homework.

rows.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào bǎ mén guān shàng.
rows.translation: Please don't close the door.

topics.title: The 被 passive
topics.description: When something happens TO the subject — usually unpleasantly

guide.intro: 被 (bèi) is the passive marker — "got / was done by". It's the mirror image of 把: where 把 puts the actor first and the patient mid-sentence, 被 puts the patient (victim) first.

sections.text: The basic shape
Pattern: Patient + 被 + (Agent) + Verb + result. The agent is optional — drop it if it's unknown or obvious.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 被 偷 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le.
rows.translation: My phone was stolen. (no agent)

rows.source: 杯子 被 他 打 破 了。
rows.pinyin: Bēizi bèi tā dǎ pò le.
rows.translation: The cup was broken by him.

rows.source: 钱 被 老板 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Qián bèi lǎobǎn ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: The money was taken by the boss.

sections.text: 把 vs 被 — same event, different POV

rows: 他 把 杯子 打 破 了
杯子 被 他 打 破 了
小偷 偷 了 我 的 手机
我 的 手机 被 (小偷) 偷 了

sections.text: Mandarin's 被 has a slightly negative or unfortunate flavor — it's used much more often for bad things (got stolen, broken, scolded) than for neutral or good ones. Sentences like "I was praised" (我 被 表扬 了) work but feel marked.
叫 / 让 — informal alternatives
In speech, 叫 (jiào) or 让 (ràng) often replace 被. They sound more casual — but unlike 被, they REQUIRE an agent.

rows.source: 我 的 钱 让 他 拿走 了。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de qián ràng tā ná zǒu le.
rows.translation: My money got taken by him.

rows.source: 他 叫 老师 批评 了。
rows.translation: He got scolded by the teacher.

sections.text: Negation
Same as 把 — put 没 BEFORE 被.

rows.source: 我 的 手机 没 被 偷。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī méi bèi tōu.
rows.translation: My phone wasn't stolen.

sections.text: Two flavors of 了
Mandarin uses 了 in two distinct slots, and 把 / 被 sentences often need both. Knowing which is which is the difference between a complete sentence and a fragment.

rows: Something is now different / new situation

rows.source: 他 吃 了 三 个 苹果。
rows.pinyin: Tā chī le sān ge píngguǒ.
rows.translation: He ate three apples. (perfective 了₁ — action complete)
It's raining now. (sentence 了₂ — change of state, didn't use to be)

rows.source: 已经 下 了 三 天 雨 了。
rows.pinyin: Yǐjīng xià le sān tiān yǔ le.
rows.translation: It's been raining for three days. (BOTH 了 — completed duration AND ongoing relevance)

sections.text: Quick test: if the 了 hugs the verb (verb 了 object), it's 了₁. If the 了 is at the very end of the sentence, it's 了₂. Same character, different jobs.

topics.title: Giving with 给
topics.description: 给 as both "give" and a coverb meaning "for / to"

guide.intro: 给 (gěi) wears two hats. As a main verb it means "give". As a coverb sitting before another verb, it marks the recipient or beneficiary — "for someone", "to someone". Both uses are everywhere.

sections.text: 给 as main verb — "give"
Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + thing. Two objects in a row, recipient first.

rows.source: 我 给 他 一 本 书。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi tā yì běn shū.
rows.translation: I gave him a book.

rows.source: 妈妈 给 我 钱。
rows.translation: Mom gave me money.

sections.text: 给 as coverb — "for / to"
Sandwiched before another verb, 给 marks who benefits or receives the action. Pattern: Subject + 给 + recipient + verb + object.

rows.source: 我 给 你 买 了 一 杯 咖啡。
rows.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ mǎi le yì bēi kāfēi.
rows.translation: I bought you a coffee. (the buying is FOR you)

rows.source: 他 给 妈妈 打 电话。
rows.translation: He's calling mom. (the call is TO mom)

rows.source: 请 给 我 介绍 一下。
rows.translation: Please introduce (it) to me.

sections.text: Notice how 给 you 买 (buy for you) and 给 妈妈 打 电话 (call mom) both keep 给 + person BEFORE the main verb. English flips this around — Chinese is rigid about the order.
Common 给-verb pairings

rows: 给 X 打 电话

topics.title: How well? — 得 complement
topics.description: Modify a verb with how it was done — 得 + adjective

guide.intro: 得 (de) lets you describe the manner or degree of an action: not WHAT you did, but HOW WELL or HOW MUCH. It's the closest Mandarin gets to English adverbs.

sections.text: The basic pattern
Pattern: Subject + Verb + 得 + (very) + Adjective. Note the position of 很 — almost always required to keep the sentence sounding natural.

rows.source: 他 跑 得 很 快。
rows.translation: He runs very fast.

rows.source: 她 唱 得 很 好。
rows.translation: She sings very well.

rows.source: 我 睡 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I didn't sleep well.

sections.text: When the verb has an object
If your verb takes an object, you have to repeat the verb. Mandarin can't have an object AND a 得 phrase on the same verb. Pattern: Subject + Verb + Object, Verb + 得 + adjective.

rows.source: 他 说 中文 说 得 很 好。
rows.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
rows.translation: He speaks Chinese very well. (literally: "speaks Chinese, speaks very well")

rows.source: 她 写 字 写 得 很 漂亮。
rows.pinyin: Tā xiě zì xiě de hěn piàoliang.
rows.translation: She writes characters beautifully.

sections.text: Common mistake: "他 说 中文 得 很 好" — wrong. The verb has to repeat. Or you can drop the object: "他 中文 说 得 很 好" also works.
Three different 得 / 的 / 地

rows: after a verb: how it was done
走 得 慢 — walks slowly

sections.text: All three are pronounced "de" (neutral tone) — only writing distinguishes them. Pay attention to position: 的 between nouns, 地 before verbs, 得 after verbs.
Negation: not 不 before 得 — 不 before the adjective

rows.source: 他 跑 得 不 快。
rows.translation: He doesn't run fast.

rows.source: 我 唱 得 不 好。
rows.translation: I don't sing well.

topics.title: Verb complements
topics.description: Resultative & directional complements — what English handles with separate words, Mandarin stitches onto the verb.

guide.intro: English says "I looked but didn't see it" with two verbs. Mandarin says 我 看 了 但 没 看见 — the result (见 = perceive) is glued to the verb (看 = look). This is the resultative complement, and it's everywhere. Directional complements work the same way but for motion.

sections.text: Resultative complements
Verb + result. The verb is the action you tried; the second character tells the outcome. Without the complement, you're only saying you DID the action, not that it WORKED.
Directional complements
Verb + direction. 上 (up), 下 (down), 进 (in), 出 (out), 回 (back), 过 (across). Compound forms add 来 (toward speaker) or 去 (away from speaker): 上来, 下去, 进来, 出去 …

rows.source: 他 走 上 楼。
rows.translation: He walks up the stairs.

rows.source: 他 走 上 来 了。
rows.translation: He walked up (toward me).

rows.source: 她 跑 出 教室。
rows.translation: She runs out of the classroom.

sections.text: Potential complement: 得 / 不

To say you CAN or CAN'T achieve the result, insert 得 (able) or 不 (not able) between the verb and the complement: 看得见 / 看不见, 听得懂 / 听不懂. This is NOT the same as 可以 + verb — that asks for permission. Potential complements ask whether the result is achievable.
English speakers reach for 可以 看见 ("can see"). That's wrong. Use 看得见 ("see-able") for "I can see it".
